$comment: The public highlighting, language and theme entry points for the in-repository library runtimes.
Rust and Elixir use snake_case; JavaScript uses camelCase. Qualified spellings put domain functions in their module.
JavaScript checks both Node and browser roots plus all language and theme module value exports in both directions.
Rust calls every listed capability and scans lib.rs and highlight.rs for unclassified functions. Elixir reflects on the root and resolves qualified module spellings.
Other module APIs are covered by their own manifests, including formatter-options.json and formatter-helpers.json.
deprecated maps a retained old spelling to its replacement. Compatibility tests check the aliases and their deprecation metadata.
Existing Rust Language methods and catalog functions remain supported alongside the shorter module functions.
Output contracts live in conformance, language-guess-cases.json, language-detection.json and theme-choice-cases.json.
Add capabilities here before implementing them and prove the runtime checks fail. runtime_only and waived entries require a reason.
The CLI exposes commands rather than library modules. The external Java binding is not scanned by these in-repository tests.

capabilities.name: closest_theme
capabilities.$comment: Find a readable built-in theme matching supplied background, foreground and ANSI colors, or return nothing.

capabilities.name: highlight
capabilities.$comment: Source plus a formatter, in, rendered output out. The one call the README leads with in every runtime.

capabilities.name: highlight_events
capabilities.$comment: The nested open/close event stream, without a formatter. Elixir lacked this until #1543.

capabilities.name: highlight_iter
capabilities.$comment: Flat per-token iteration: text, language, range, scope, resolved style. Waived for Elixir below.

capabilities.name: guess
capabilities.$comment: Resolve a name, an alias or a path to a language, falling back to plain text.

capabilities.name: available_languages
capabilities.$comment: Every language in the catalog, with its aliases and extensions.

capabilities.name: available_themes
capabilities.$comment: Every built-in theme's name and appearance.

capabilities.name: language_info
capabilities.$comment: One language looked up by id or alias, without scanning the catalog.

capabilities.name: theme
capabilities.$comment: Look up a built-in theme by exact name. Absence uses the runtime's existing missing-value convention.

$comment: Entry points one runtime publishes at the top level and the others should
not, because the boundary dictates it rather than taste. Each entry says
why, and the tests fail on a name here that the runtime no longer exports,
so the list cannot outlive its reasons.
"Only this runtime" is about the top level. Where another runtime has the
same capability somewhere else, the reason says where.

rust.write_highlight: Streams into a `&mut dyn Write`, so a large document never exists as one `String`. JavaScript builds strings and Elixir returns iodata the caller hands to Phoenix; neither has a writer to stream into.

javascript.createHighlighter: Splits async setup from synchronous rendering, because loading a parser is a promise here. Rust's `lumis::highlight::Highlighter` is a type rather than an entry point, and Elixir's NIF loads inside `highlight/2`, so neither has an async phase to split off.
javascript.languages.load: Warms the shared parser runtime by name. Elixir exposes Languages.load/1 and async_load/1; Rust selects grammars at compile time.
javascript.languages.loaded: Reports the languages loaded into the shared runtime; the counterpart of Languages.loaded in Elixir. Rust grammars are selected at compile time.
javascript.runtimeKind: Reports whether the Wasmtime addon or `web-tree-sitter` is highlighting. JavaScript alone ships both runtimes in one package; the CLI, Elixir and Rust each have exactly one, so there is nothing to ask.
javascript.languages.withWasm: Attaches a parser package imported as a namespace to a language. A package's default export is already the language, so this is only for code that imports the package some other way. Rust compiles grammars in, and the CLI and Elixir read and verify them at run time, so neither has packages to import.
javascript.languages.configureWasmResolver: Overrides where parser assets are fetched from. Elixir configures that with `config :lumis, :parser_dirs` and the CLI with its config file, neither of which is a function.

elixir.default_options: The validated default keyword list. Options are a `NimbleOptions` schema here, so a caller can read the defaults back; Rust's are a typed builder's `Default` and JavaScript's an object literal, neither of which is a function.
elixir.validate_options!: Checks a keyword list against the same schema before `highlight/2` does, so a caller can fail early on user input. Rust's builder and JavaScript's types reject the same mistakes at compile time.
elixir.Languages.loaded: Reports the languages loaded into the VM. See languages.loaded under javascript.

$comment: A canonical capability a runtime does not offer. Each entry carries its
reason and, where it is a gap rather than a boundary, the issue tracking
it. The tests fail on a waiver the runtime has since grown, so it can only
shrink.
Unlike `formatter-options.json` and `formatter-helpers.json`, whose tests
assert this section is empty, this one starts with an entry. It is the gap
#1544 was opened about.

elixir.highlight_iter: Not implemented. Rust has `highlight_iter/4` and JavaScript has `highlightIter`; Elixir has no flat per-token walk, only the nested stream from `highlight_events/3`. It is implementable on top of that, so this waiver is a gap and not a boundary, and dropping it is the point.
